articleTitle: Virtual private network control system concept
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: NTT has offered the advanced network service system to satisfy customer demand for new services in a timely manner and also has proposed a hierarchical network data management system called the advanced network service support system. Recently, demand for network service flexibility has been increasing especially in the business environment. The virtual private network service, which allows users to define their own network structure, numbering plan, traffic control and billing conditions on the public network, can satisfy these demands. This service can be realized by the network function virtualizing technique based on the hierarchical network data management architecture, and enables service definition on a logical service network independently of the switching network structure and functions. It can be said that a kind of operating system (OS) for network control needs to be built that provides new services that are independent of network feature components. In this paper, virtual network control architecture is discussed and the virtual private network service is outlined as a typical application.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: ISDN multimedia desk top teleconferencing
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: Describes an internal AT&T trial application utilizing unique capabilities of ISDN. The following application design criteria was chosen for this trial; it must: consist of an end user application which would be both easy to use and to understand; contain as much common office communications equipment as possible; and incorporate ISDN capabilities which would increase the usefulness of the application over that provided by current telecommunications capabilities. The trial equipment included a prototype multimedia desk top workstation which provides for the simultaneous transmission of voice, data and still frame, bit mapped images. The networking capabilities of these workstations are supported by a terminal interface which can interwork with the ISDN protocol and is supported on both private line PBX networks, and on public switched networks. The following three components that comprise a desk top multimedia teleconference in the ISDN environment are described: the workstation equipment; the ISDN teleconferencing application software that runs on the workstations; and the ISDN switched network, consisting of both virtual private line and physical private line network services, that interconnect these workstations.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Interactive Home Systems (IHS)-an overview
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: IHS is a 2-year collaborative project under the EUREKA umbrella, whose purpose is to define a European standard by which domestic appliances may be interconnected via a common bus network. Seven leading companies are involved, namely Thorn-EMI, GEC, Mullard, Philips, Siemens, Electrolux and Thompson. These companies together hold a substantial proportion of the European market for domestic electrical equipment and have the combined strength to set standards. This paper presents a brief overview of the work so far and describes some envisaged applications.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Private ISDN
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: Summarises the reasons behind a company's decision to invest in a private network. Today private networks are composed of separate building blocks rather than integrated building blocks. For local area applications LANs and PABXs are the main building blocks. Voice applications can only adequately be covered by a PABX. With a modern PABX voice and data can be integrated as well. With the advent of modern signalling systems PABX functionality can also be extended to be offered in networks. Data services offered by the PABX can be an alternative for terminal distribution primarily for low frequency users of data. User with stringent requirements on data speeds for file transfer etc. are best served by a LAN or a dedicated data network. For wide area data, aspects leased lines are used along with public data network services such as circuit or packet switched data.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Architecture of hierarchical integrated LAN based on FDDI
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: The Fibre Distributed Data Interface (FDDI), proposed by the ANSI as a high-speed interface standard within large scale computer systems, is expected to be adopted as an integrative means of communication among LANs. This integrative means is termed 'backbone LAN' and each 802 LAN is termed 'branch LAN'. Furthermore, the system, hierarchically consisting of a backbone LAN and its branch LANs, is termed 'hierarchical integrated local area network (HI LAN)'. First of all HI LANs architecture is presented, namely the concept, the model, the communication protocols, the communication methods for internal relaying among branch LANs through a backbone LAN. Then the implementation techniques based on HI LANs concept are described. Finally the relaying efficiency is evaluated with respect to each different address system assigned to the terminals in branch LANs.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Virtual private networks
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: Virtual private networks is a concept that will have a significant impact on the future of business communications. The virtual private network (VPN) offers a fresh, innovative approach to the traditional problem of supplying efficient, reliable, easy to use telecommunications for large, geographically dispersed groups of subscribers. VPN replaces existing private networks with a flexible architecture that is easily managed and at the same time provides enhanced services. As the number of business locations in the private network increases, so do the interconnect requirements and the network complexity. Traffic engineering and network management become more important and more costly. Indeed some large private networks can exceed the size and complexity of smaller PTTs. It is here that the virtual private network first shows its benefits allowing the private networks' operation to retain an apparently simple network without any loss of interconnect functionality.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Workload characterization in PBX performance studies
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: The authors study the question of adequate workload characterization in the context of a PBX capacity modeling effort. In particular, they address the question of the accuracy which can be expected from such a study, if the 'burstyness' inherent in the calling process is ignored. Although the results obtained are somewhat sensitive to the processor software architecture, they assume an architecture that is simple and quite realistic for PBX systems of small and moderate size. State-of-the-art simulation and analytic tools are employed in this study.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Modern voice/data network design in the complex American commercial environment
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: Fiber optic systems are effecting a revolution in the long-haul transmission world. The architectural impact of the use of high-bandwidth fiber-optic backbones and digital cross-connect equipment changes the conventional perspective towards backbone and access-line design. In this paper, the value of a unique family of personal computer (PC) based network analysis and design tools to assist in these choices is illustrated. The US Department of Treasury's voice and data requirements are used as the basis for a case study of the effect of these new products and services.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Business networks and ISDN
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: The authors examine some of the characteristics of major business networks today, and consider how improvements in network capabilities can address the needs of business network managers and their users. An example of a business network is presented, showing how a feature such as a uniform dialing plan can lead to more efficient use of network resources and more effective use of the business network user's time. The role and impact of ISDN (Integrated Services Digital Network) technology on business communications is discussed. In particular, they consider how one component of ISDN-Primary Rate Access-can act as a bridge between public and private networks to provide effective communication for the 1990s.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Digital networking
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: To provide businesses with effective communications and management of information resources, Northern Telecom recently announced its corporate networking solution-Meridian Customer Defined Networking. This broad portfolio of products, applications, and customer support tools for corporate networking gives businesses of all sizes and complexity the freedom to create their own powerful hybrid networks. It establishes, for the first time, a peer-to-peer level of interworking between private and public networks, based on industry standard Integrated Services Digital Network (ISDN) and Common Channel Signalling System number 7 (CCS7) protocols and interfaces. This peer relationship allows a fully featured private network to appear as an equal partner to a fully featured public network (with the public network viewed as many 'virtual' private networks that also provide Centrex type services), and also to a fully featured long-distance network.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Innovative developments in dedicated circuits for PABX applications
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: Describes a solid-state subscriber line interface circuit (SLIC) designed by SGS-Thompson Microelectronics to eliminate the high amplitude transients caused by relay contact bounce. This SLIC developed for analogue cards consists of two devices: the L3000, realised in HV technology that interfaces directly to the line; and the L3090, which integrates all of the control and system interface functions. In the PABX sector, a frequently requested function is the conference call. This function is possible with a single chip due to VLSI technology. The integrated digital PCM processor developed by SGS-Thompson can receive up to 32 channels from the TDM input highway and accepts all the basic rates: 1536, 1544, and 2048 kbit/s.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A multi-site videophone PBX system
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: This paper looks at the design of a multi-site PBX videophone system in terms of technology choices for transmission, switching and call-control, and considers the system in relation to future IPBX- and ISDN-based videophone systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Corporate networking standards
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: Examines the three main groups of layered corporate networking protocols: open system interconnection (OSI protocols), ISDN access protocols; and IBM's System Network Architecture (SNA) protocols. Work in standards organisations will continue toward reconciling the three major group of protocols. Meanwhile, these organisations are also focusing on protocol performance. The evolution of generally accepted corporate networking standards will focus on three specific areas of any network's operation; user access to the network, interfaces within the network, and interfaces between one network and other networks.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Regulatory considerations for digital private networks in the UK
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: Liberalisation of private telecommunications equipment supply over recent years in the UK has resulted in a new regulatory regime, new product standards and operating licences. The introduction of new public digital services and the increasing availability of digital private switching systems integrating voice and data have accelerated the move towards fully digital private networks, coincidental with the introduction of the Integrated Services Digital Network (ISDN). It is important for all suppliers of apparatus and operators of such networks in the UK to be aware of current regulatory considerations. With an emphasis on digital private networks intending to use public network services, this paper outlines the current regulatory regime in the UK. The background to some of the more important product standards is revealed, and the importance of Oftel's Private Network Code of Practice examined in some depth.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Flexible network access structure applicable to versatile terminal distribution patterns
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: This paper, first, presents a new circuit switching-oriented, high-speed, multiple-access passive bus interface, which is well suited to PBX (private branch exchange) applications where voice communications dominate. It then describes the impacts the new interface poses on the extension wiring system and proposes several schemes to cope with the problems of increasingly complex wiring arrangements and bottlenecks to achieving reliably and to expand its bare capabilities.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Integration of voice and data traffic for international corporate network
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: Voice digitization techniques such as PCM or ADPCM usually employed in domestic private network requires 64 or 32 kbps speed for a single voice channel transmission and it is still expensive for an international private network. KDD laboratory has developed a highly efficient and good quality voice codec. Using this codec and employing a highly efficient multiplexing technique, KDD has developed a system called ICX (Intelligent Circuit Exchange) which can integrate voice and data traffic efficiently and economically. This paper describes the design principles and functions of the ICX which is under installation for commercial use, and presents an international private network configuration using the ICX.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Frame Relaying Service opportunity
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: The Frame Relaying Service will provide the opportunity to offer packet-like frame transmission service at the Link Layer (layer 2 of the OSI model) at speeds up to 1.5 Mbps. Frame Relaying will be able to minimize processing overhead and allow for fast switching speeds and greater throughput. The initial application of the Frame Relaying service is expected to be the interconnection of local area networks (LANs) and personal computers (PCs) which inherently possess their own higher layer functions, such as flow control and error recovery capabilities. Frame Relaying can convey LAN frames basically unchanged or with minimal changes between communicating LANs. The ease of inter-LAN and PC to PC connections is a significant advantage and may become a critical characteristic of the potential service.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Flexibility of private networks-a user's viewpoint
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: The Belgian Gendarmerie has recently installed its nationwide private PABX network, based on 60 PABX, which are currently being linked by (also private) 2 Mbit links. This network covers all the telecommunication needs between fixed points for voice as well as for data, text and document transmission. After a description of the network and its multiple functions, attention is paid to the special functionalities of the voice and data networks, as well as of the network management system, which is being studied. This will show that the digital PABX is in fact a powerful communications computer offering a lot of flexibility and can run very specific tasks in order to meet the particular needs of any organization.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Communicating with the high street
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: The Boots Company plc are currently developing an integrated digital network supported by digital PABXs capable of meeting the requirements of the business both present and future. The purpose of this paper is to outline the requirements of the business and how regulatory and technological changes impact upon their provision. It concludes by suggesting how these requirements may develop and how corporations should best position themselves to take maximum benefit in the future.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Private network services on System X
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: Discusses the Centrex and virtual private network (VPN) facilities of System X which can be used in the business communications environment. These together as a private network service offer alternatives to the traditional solutions for voice and data communications in corporate networks.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Customer initiated service assurance for private networks
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: Describes a plan to implement performance, fault, and configuration management features that are directly related to service assurance in the current private network environment. Typical service configurations are presented to demonstrate how end users can monitor, test, and directly control the transmission quality of their networks.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Development of an integrated system for automated network administration: a case study
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: At the University of Liverpool, the central computing services department, the Computer Laboratory, is developing and maintaining computer networks to provide campus wide computing facilities. The department is responsible for running systems to support undergraduate teaching, research, general university administration and various support services such as the library and building maintenance departments. Each aspect of the service is run on a different machine (or machines). Support is also offered for microcomputer users across a range of machines and recently a number of self contained (20/30 workstation) local area networks (LANs) for teaching have been established. This paper describes techniques which are being developed by the University Computer Laboratory to administer its complex and rapidly growing network of equipment.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Analysis of the relationship between PABX, LAN and ISDN primary access
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: Compares the capabilities of dedicated PABX with those of LAN and integrated PABX/LAN solutions, under the ISDN scenario. The digital PABX will be probably the most suitable solution for private communication needs and LANs are very effective for specific applications like CPU disks traffic, CAD/CAM and factory automation. The strengths and weaknesses of the dedicated data PABX are compared to those of the LAN and integrated data/voice PABX with respect to its suitability in ISDN environment.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A model for assessing the ability of an office local area network, employing the Technical Office Protocol (TOP) to carry interactive speech while heavily loaded with data traffic
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: In a move towards optimising office procedure the modern generation of office information systems are adopting local area networks (LANs) as the means of supporting the distributed computer systems being employed to provide electronic mail, word processing and file transfers facilities. As a result, various computer networks have been suggested to support these activities. Currently emerging standards tend to favour carrier sense multiple access collision detection (CSMA/CD) with Technical Office Protocol (TOP) for office automation. In addition to the transfer of data between workstations and processors a need has been established for verbal communication between users of the network on an interactive basis. PABXs already provide this facility but this necessitates the provision of a completely separate cabling network and exchange. It is proposed that LANs can provide the interactive speech facility in addition to the data handling capability and thus obviate the need for PABX.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Extending ISDN functional layering concepts in PBX architectures
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: Introduces and defines the concept of functional layering in PBX architectures. The evolutionary stages of functional layering are described, beginning with current PBXs that have limited functional layering and ending with a proposed PBX architecture with functional layering extended beyond ISDN standards. Additionally, advantages of functional layering are described, along with current standards and technology trends that indicate extended functional layering will be realized in the future.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Integrated messaging services in an ISDN PBX network
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: This paper describes a set of advanced messaging features, all integrated into a comprehensive messaging service on the PBX. It then proposes functional application of these services across PBX networks. ISDN D-channel signaling is used as the vehicle for inter-PBX communication. Thus, if PBXs support standard messaging functions, and if they interconnect with standard interfaces using standard signaling protocols, then enhanced messaging services can be offered in multivendor PBX networks.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The integration of private and public networks
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: Recommendations and standards are emerging from bodies such as the CCITT regarding the nature of the Integrated Services Digital Network (ISDN). With changes taking place regarding the regulations on establishing and operating a private network, many Corporations are preparing for the networks of the future. This paper examines the history; the evolution to present day technology; the future trends; and summarises the role of the modern PABX in the ISDN.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Limits of the ISDN S-interface
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: The limits of the ISDN S-interface are determined for the short passive bus, extended bus and point-to-point wiring configurations by means of a computer simulation. The simulation can be used as a tool in projecting an in-house installation. The model for simulating the S-bus is based on the well-known theory of transmission line. With an interactive program an ultimate bus configuration can be found which still meets the requirements of the CCITT specifications I.430 and of the received minimum eye opening at the network termination (NT). The latter is related to a bit error rate objective of the interface. The length of the bus, the length of the cords, the number of terminals and their places on the bus are input variables to the program. The transmitter output impedance, the receiver input impedance and the cable parameters are taken into account as frequency-dependent variables in the program.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An ISDN signalling system for private networks
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: With the imminent arrival of public ISDN services in Australia, Telecom Australia-PABX Unit has developed TeLinc, an ISDN signalling system for private networks, to allow flexible networking of PABXs using public ISDN resources and to support a wide range of supplementary services with feature transparency across private networks. TeLinc allows private networks in the ISDN to be realized economically taking full advantage of ISDN functionality and to evolve without the undue constraint of being tied to a single vendor irrespective of performance and cost criteria. The paper outlines the scope of the signalling system and the protocol structure for various scenarios. Individual layer protocols as well as supplementary services supported in the signalling system are also discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Experience gained from the implementation of DASS and DPNSS
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: Before dealing with the experience of the application of DASS and DPNSS and their differences a summary of the history and a general description of these signalling systems is given. The Digital Access Signalling System (DASS) was conceived in 1981 as the signalling system for the Integrated Digital Access to the public telephone network in advance of any internationally accepted standards. DASS is designed to provide signalling service both to basic rate access and to primary rate access users. DPNSS was conceived during 1983 as a signalling system to enable large corporate network users to create a 'private ISDN'. The DPNSS specification was developed by a number of parties with the intention of creating an 'Open System' such that a number of implementations could be seen to work together, offering the customer the freedom to choose the 'best' PABX/ISPBX to meet the specific requirements of a given site. As a long term aim this has been achieved by careful specification to allow flexibility.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: CorNet: Siemens' contribution to the standardization of signaling in corporate ISDN networks
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: To make possible a complete integration of all telecommunication functions and to allow for the network-wide control of supplementary services, private networks are combined to form corporate ISDN networks. CorNet is the comprehensive protocol for signalling in such corporate ISDN networks. The authors explain the intentions of CorNet, clarify its relationship to other national or international ISDN protocol specifications and demonstrate some of the new features which were introduced with CorNet. CorNet is definitely committed to CCITT standards. It specifies how these standards apply for communication in corporate networks, and what additional extensions are required to satisfy the demands of private signalling.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A new system with distributed architecture suitable for business applications
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: XLNET is a fully distributed LAN that combines the advantages of a traditional PABX and a LAN. As such it has been conceived to meet the needs of a modern business in that it handles mixed traffic (voice, data, etc.) in a transparent way and that in a normal environment it is virtually outage free. There is currently a need to provide switching facilities that: could handle mixed traffic in a transparent way, be virtually outage free, and be capable of meeting the future as well as current business needs. XLNET has been conceived with these aspects in mind. It is a fault tolerant and rugged system that integrates a variety of services. Distributed architecture and integration of the switching is a feature of the XLNET. Integration occurs at all levels of the architecture using packet switching allowing system capacity to be dynamically shared among the users.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The digital PBX: current and future views of applications for information management
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: The digital PBX, viewed as an office controller for integration of voice and data on the premises and as a gateway for wide area interpremises networking, is finding increased application in today's business and campus environments. The paper discusses the role of the digital PBX in connecting data end points of various types (asynchronous, synchronous, peer-to-peer) both locally and over wide areas through examination of typical end customer applications. Two specific customer scenarios are considered: a multi-location, interpremises data networking application and a large, single campus, research institution with intensive computational and intrapremises information movement requirements. In looking forward, the approach is to discuss the migration of the PBX to ISDN technology and to evaluate future synergies between the ISDN PBX and network services offerings. From this perspective, the digital PBX is seen as assuming an expanded role in satisfying the information movement and management needs of end users in the coming decade.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Hybrid approach for the design of a broadband local area network
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: Present a new broadband LAN/MAN architecture, called INFONET. INFONET is based on a unidirectional bus physical topology. In this structure each type of traffic uses a different logical topology and a different transfer technique as well. For isochronous traffic (V traffic) e.g. video and PCM voice, a synchronous transfer mode, operating on a logical ring structure, has been selected; whereas a logical bus topology and ATM are associated with the nonisochronous traffic (D traffic) e.g. data and packetized voice. The main characteristics of INFONET are presented, and details on implementation of synchronous and asynchronous transfer modes (ATM) in the network structure are discussed. The main features of the medium access procedures and results of a performance evaluation study are also presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The British Steel Corporation-integrated digital network
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: The British Steel Corporation (BSC) has been operating one of the most extensive private telecommunications systems in the UK, for the past ten years. This system gives BSC considerable cost savings, as well as offering significant functional, performance and security advantages. This system is known as COTEN (Corporate Telecommunications Network). The heart of the BSC system is the COTEN transmission network shown. This is a high capacity, modern, digital network that links the main centres of Corporate activity. This system can support the transmission of all types of information (data, speech, text, graphics) via three subordinate telecommunications services: a private COTEN data network linking four large IBM mainframe installations (at Aldwarke, Port Talbot, Teesside and Corby); a private COTEN speech network offering desk-to-desk dialling throughout most of the Corporation; and a COTEN terminal connection service linking remote terminal systems to their host IBM or ICL mainframes, or to minicomputers, on multiple sites.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The emergence of the 'network company'
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: British Telecom has been providing networking products to its customers for nearly twenty years. The market for these products has seen dramatic changes in the last few years. The early multiplexers available only a few years ago compare very unfavourably-in terms of both features and appearance-with today's sophisticated products. Like most items of electronic equipment they have also dropped in price. As a result of this and the parallel developments in price and availability of computing power a number of companies have been able to install major telecommunications or computer networks and use them in a way which fundamentally changes the nature of their business. These are 'network companies' for whom telecommunications have assumed a strategic priority.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Managing the multi-functional network
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: Network management is one of the more ambiguous terms in use by communications specialists today. It has a kind of Alice in Wonderland-'it means what I want it to mean'-appeal to marketiers visibly trying to differentiate their PABX or data communication products. Most people would recognise the vital importance of manageable network systems, but there are still too few areas of common understanding or standards to make the term safe to use in well regulated company. The author offers a view of what network management really means, biased from a knowledge of where voice and data management systems have come from. It is orientated very much towards the view that networked systems management is the ultimate goal of all parties involved.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: How expert systems can support network diagnostics, management and control
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: The purpose of this paper is to: briefly review the typical networking situation and related problems and consequences that have to be considered in network management environments; give an insight into the characteristics and the functionality that can be derived from using expert systems, how they can help and support networking operations, and how they differ from conventional systems; show specifically how expert systems can most effectively be applied to improve network diagnostic, management and support capabilities; provide practical examples on the strategic options that might be available to most effectively improve network operational capabilities; resolving a considerable range of support problems which include both trivial and complex diagnostic issues, online and remote problem determination to identify immediate and potential problems, down to a component, line and sub-component level; and indicate the costs, benefits and the conclusions that can be drawn from considering the use of expert systems to support network management and control.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Communications network management-the CEGB perspective
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: The Central Electricity Generating Board (the Board) generates, transmits and supplies electric power in bulk to 12 Area Distribution Boards in England and Wales in the UK. The Board has been implementing a strategy of integrated telecommunications and operates a large private network, called the Corporate Communications Network (CCN), which uses digital and analogue technology to support voice and point-to-point data requirements. This paper examines the requirements for network management within the Board, describes existing and planned network management systems, relates the Board's experience of managing and operating a private network and discusses the future of network management within a multivendor environment.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: ISDN applications in the business environment
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: Reviews the infrastructure which is being established through the initial implementation of ISDN. Then, the present communications environment of a hypothetical business customer is characterized. The communications environment of this customer is advanced, but represents the composite networking situation at many of today's leading-edge companies. The possible enhancements to the company communications environment and operating efficiency which can be achieved through use of a variety of ISDN applications are examined. Since this is a composite scenario, these benefits would apply to virtually all companies using private networks.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: User services requirements for distributed information technology networks
publicationTitle: 1988 International Conference on Private Switching Systems and Networks
abstract: This paper is intended to promote discussion about the properties required from future distributed information systems, if they are to meet the needs of users. It is based on the authors' experience of analysing users' problems and requirements, of applying the kinds of services which are now available, and of assessing the impact of emerging technology. The discussion is centred on the idea of a distributed information technology network (DITN), which offers Open Systems Interconnection services to a multiplicity of users. It is assumed that future economies of scale will be so dominant that shared DITNs are bound to be created to serve groups of organisations. User requirements and related aspects in a DITN are considered under four main headings: user services requirements; network services requirements; service evolution requirements; and network management and control.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
